label: Constitutional Analysis
sentences: The question here falls under Article I, Section 1. The lawmaking powers the Constitution grants are given to Congress, which is a Senate and a House. It reads: “All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives.”
This story is about telecom equipment failing and halting departures nationwide.
The Constitution, signed on September 17, 1787, says "All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress of the United States."
The Constitution, signed on September 17, 1787, lets Congress make the laws needed to carry out powers vested in the Government of the United States "or in any Department or Officer thereof."

In March 1788, in The Federalist No. 72 (March 1788) Alexander Hamilton wrote that matters like "The actual conduct of foreign negotiations, the preparatory plans of finance, the application and disbursement of the public moneys in conformity to the general appropriations of the legislature" belong to the administration of government, and that the persons to whose immediate management they are committed "ought to be considered as the assistants or deputies of the chief magistrate."
Planes in the air could land, and the FAA said, "All departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice."
The strongest argument against this is that the stop was only temporary helper work under unrepealed rules already made, not new lawmaking.
We read this clause to mean Congress alone holds the lawmaking powers the Constitution grants.
We read this clause to mean an agency may set a stop for all only under power Congress has given.
Power does not move to an agency on its own.
